8                     UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                           
9                   SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA                          
10                                                                            
11  PACIFIC VIBRATIONS, LLC,             Case No.:  22cv1118-LL-DDL           

12                             Plaintiff,                                     
                                        ORDER GRANTING IN PART AND           
13  v.                                   DENYING IN PART DEFENDANT            
                                        SLOW GOLD LIMITED’S MOTION           
14  SLOW GOLD LIMITED, et al.,                                                
                                        FOR LEAVE TO FILE                    
15                          Defendants.  COUNTERCLAIMS                        

16                                                                            
                                        [ECF No. 14]                         
17                                                                            
18       Before the Court is Defendant Slow Gold Limited’s Motion for Leave to File 
19  Counterclaims  against  Plaintiff  Pacific  Vibrations,  LLC.  ECF  No.  14  (“Motion”  or 
20  “Mot.”).  Plaintiff  filed  an  Opposition  [ECF  No.  19  (“Opposition”  or  “Oppo.”)],  and 
21  Defendant Slow Gold Limited (“Defendant”) filed a Reply [ECF No. 21 (“Reply”)]. The 
22  Court took this matter under submission without oral argument pursuant to Civil Local 
23  Rule  7.1(d)(1).  For  the  reasons  stated  below,  the  Court  GRANTS  IN  PART  AND 
24  DENIES IN PART Defendant’s Motion.                                        
25  I.   BACKGROUND                                                           
26       On March 11, 2022, Plaintiff filed a complaint in state court against Defendants 
27  Slow Gold Limited, Simon Charles Tucker, Cassie Green, and Bradley John Hockridge 
28  alleging the following causes of action: (1) breach of contract; (2) unfair competition,  
1  (3) federal trademark infringement, (4) California common law trademark infringement, 
2  and (5) false designation of origin. ECF No. 1-2 at 5–27.                 
3       On July 29, 2022, Defendant filed its notice of removal and its answer. ECF Nos. 1; 
4  1-2 at 29–38; 5.                                                          
5       The parties participated in a meet-and-confer phone call on August 15, 2022, in 
6  which Defendant advised that it wished to file a counterclaim. ECF No. 14-1, Declaration 
7  of Thomas J. Speiss, III (“Speiss Decl.”), ¶ 3; ECF No. 19-1, Declaration of Ryan J. 
8  Altomare (“Altomare Decl.”), ¶ 3.                                         
9       On October 17, 2022, the Court issued a scheduling order setting pretrial deadlines, 
10  including a filing deadline of December 2, 2022 for any motion to join other parties, to 
11  amend the pleadings, or to file additional pleadings. ECF No. 11 at 1. The deadline to 
12  complete fact discovery was set for May 5, 2023. Id. at 2.                
13       On December 1, 2022, Defendant provided a copy of its proposed counterclaims to 
14  Plaintiff. Speiss Decl. ¶ 5; Altomare Decl. ¶ 10.                         
15       On December 2, 2022, Defendant filed this Motion seeking leave to amend its 
16  answer to add counterclaims against Plaintiff. ECF No. 14.                
17  II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                       
18       Once a party has served its pleading, there is a short period of time when the party 
19  may amend it once as a matter of right. Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(1). In all other cases, a party 
20  may amend its pleading only with written consent from the opposing party or permission 
21  from the court. Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2). “The court should freely give leave when justice 
22  so requires.” Id. This policy should be applied with “extreme liberality” to reflect the 
23  underlying purpose of Rule 15 “to facilitate decision on the merits, rather than on the 
24  pleadings or technicalities.” United States v. Webb, 655 F.2d 977, 979 (9th Cir. 1981).  
25       Leave to amend should be granted absent a showing of “undue delay, bad faith or 
26  dilatory motive, futility of amendment, and prejudice to the opposing party.” Id. at 980 
27  (citing Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178, 182 (1962)). Prejudice to the opposing party is the 
28  factor that carries the greatest weight. Eminence Cap., LLC v. Aspeon, Inc., 316 F.3d 1048, 
1  1052 (9th Cir. 2003). “Absent prejudice, or a strong showing of any of the remaining 
2  Foman factors, there exists a presumption under Rule 15(a) in favor of granting leave to 
3  amend.” Id. “The party opposing amendment bears the burden of showing prejudice.” DCD 
4  Programs, Ltd. v. Leighton, 833 F.2d 183, 187 (9th Cir. 1987).            
5  III.  DISCUSSION                                                          
6       Defendant argues that it should be allowed to amend its answer to file counterclaims 
7  because (1) it detrimentally relied on Plaintiff’s representation concerning Defendant’s 
8  request for stipulation to its filing of counterclaims and (2) it is appropriate at this early 
9  stage in the litigation. Mot. at 10–11. The counterclaims that Defendant seeks to add are 
10  breach of contract and declaratory judgment of non-infringement of trademark. Id. at 6; 
11  ECF No. 14-2 at 10–11. Plaintiff claims that both of Defendant’s arguments fail and leave 
12  to amend should be denied.                                                
13       A.   Detrimental Reliance                                            
14       Plaintiff and Defendant disagree about what occurred at a meet-and-confer between 
15  counsel in August 2022. Defense counsel Thomas Speiss claims that Melissa Wilner, a 
16  colleague who no longer works at his firm, had met and conferred with Plaintiff’s counsel 
17  Ryan  Altomare  about  Defendant’s  proposed  counterclaims  and  provided  an  oral  and 
18  written summary of the meeting to him. Speiss Decl. ¶ 3. Defendant claims Mr. Altomare 
19  stated, inter alia, that he did not “have any objections” to the counterclaim and requested 
20  a copy of the counterclaim prior to stipulating to its filing. Id. When Defendant provided a 
21  copy of the counterclaims almost four months later, Plaintiff declined to stipulate to their 
22  filing.  Id.  ¶  5.  Defendant  claims  it  detrimentally  relied  on  this  unfulfilled  promise.  
23  Mot. at 11.                                                               
24       Plaintiff’s counsel, on the other hand, denies that he said he had no objections to the 
25  proposed counterclaims. Altomare Decl. ¶ 3. Mr. Altomare attests that he told Ms. Wilner 
26  during the meet-and-confer phone call that he did not have authority to stipulate to the 
27  counterclaims, but he would be willing to review a draft and discuss with his client if it 
28  would be something his client would stipulate to. Id. Plaintiff filed an objection to the 
1  portion of Mr. Speiss’s declaration conveyed to him by Ms. Wilner as inadmissible hearsay 
2  and for lack of personal knowledge. ECF No. 20. Defendant made no response to the 
3  objection.                                                                
4       The Court is not persuaded by Defendant’s detrimental reliance claim. The Court 
5  agrees with Plaintiff that Ms. Wilmer’s “oral and written summary” to Mr. Speiss is 
6  inadmissible hearsay pursuant to Federal Rule of Evidence 802. Defendant did not submit 
7  a declaration by Ms. Wilmer, and Mr. Speiss lacked personal knowledge of the phone 
8  conversation at issue pursuant to Federal Rule of Evidence 602. The Court therefore 
9  sustains Plaintiff’s objection to a portion of paragraph 3 of Mr. Speiss’s declaration.1 
10  Accordingly,  Defendant’s  detrimental  reliance  argument  fails  with  the  absence  of  a 
11  promise made by Plaintiff.                                                
12       The Court will next consider the Foman factors of undue delay, bad faith or dilatory 
13  motive, futility of amendment, and prejudice to the opposing party.       
14       B.   Undue Delay and Prejudice                                       
15       Defendant claims that it did not unduly delay in filing this Motion four months after 
16  it removed this matter to federal court and that Plaintiff will not be prejudiced by granting 
17  its Motion because discovery is still ongoing. Mot. at 13–15; Reply at 6–8. Plaintiff argues 
18  that Defendant has failed to provide a reasonable explanation for filing this Motion four 
19  months after it filed its answer when the counterclaims are based on facts and theories 
20  Defendant knew or should have known at the time it filed its answer. Oppo. at 11. Plaintiff 
21                                                                            

22                                                                            
23  1 The Court sustains Plaintiff’s objection to the following:              
        My  colleague,  Melissa  Wilner,  who  no  longer  works  for  Buchalter, 
24                                                                            
        participated in this meeting at my direction and provided an oral and written 
25       summary  of  the  meeting  to  me.  Ryan  Altomare,  counsel  for  Plaintiff, 
        participated in this meeting. During the meeting, Plaintiff’s counsel requested 
26                                                                            
        a copy of the counterclaim prior to stipulating to its filing, stated that he 
27       understood “that these motions typically get granted at this stage,” and stated 
        that he did not “have any objections” to the counterclaim.           
28                                                                            
1  further contends that it will be prejudiced if this Motion is granted because it will increase 
2  the discovery required to be conducted and may require supplemental responses, which 
3  will drive up litigation costs. Id. at 17–18.                             
4       “Undue delay is delay that prejudices the nonmoving party or imposes unwarranted 
5  burdens on the court.” Davis v. Powell, 901 F. Supp. 2d 1196, 1212 (S.D. Cal. 2012) 
6  (quoting BNSF Ry. Co. v. San Joaquin Valley R. Co., No. 1:08-CV-01086-AWI, 2011 WL 
7  3328398, at *2 (E.D. Cal. Aug. 2, 2011)).                                 
8       The Court finds Defendant has not unduly delayed in filing this Motion. Although 
9  Defendant first informed Plaintiff of its intention to file counterclaims about four months 
10  prior to filing this Motion, the delay is not unreasonably long. See Howey v. United States, 
11  481 F.2d 1187, 1191 (9th Cir. 1973) (finding a district court had abused its discretion in 
12  denying leave to amend five years after the original pleadings in the absence of bad faith 
13  or prejudice and stating that “the mere fact that the government could have moved at an 
14  earlier time to amend does not by itself constitute an adequate basis for denying leave to 
15  amend.”). The instant Motion was timely filed according to the party’s case scheduling 
16  order for pretrial matters, and fact discovery will not close until May 2023. Although 
17  discovery has begun, it is in its early stages and will continue for several months. The Court 
18  does not find that allowing counterclaims at this stage of the litigation will prejudice 
19  Plaintiff or burden the Court. The Court’s finding of no undue delay and no prejudice 
20  weighs toward granting the Motion.                                        
21       C.   Bad Faith                                                       
22       Defendant contends that it brings this Motion in good faith because its counterclaims 
23  have merit and directly relate to the contract at issue in Plaintiff’s complaint. Mot. at 9. 
24  Plaintiff argues that Defendant has shown bad faith by misstating Plaintiff’s purported 
25  “consent” to add counterclaims and for delaying its filing of this Motion in an effort to 
26  harass Plaintiff and/or increase the costs of litigation. Oppo. at 13.    
27       The Court does not find that Plaintiff has established that Defendant has acted in bad 
28  faith.  Although  Defendant  may  have  misstated  Plaintiff’s  purported  consent  to  the 
1  counterclaims, the Court has not considered or relied on the purported consent in its 
2  analysis. The Court has already found that although Defendant could have filed this Motion 
3  earlier, the delay was not unreasonable, and it was timely according to the parties’ case 
4  scheduling order. Furthermore, the parties appear to agree that Defendant’s proposed 
5  counterclaims are compulsory.2 Mot. at 12; Oppo. at 5. The Court agrees that Defendant’s 
6  proposed counterclaims are compulsory because they arise out of the agreement that is the 
7  subject  matter  of  Plaintiff’s  complaint.  If  Defendant  fails  to  plead  a  compulsory 
8  counterclaim, it will be precluded from asserting it in a separate action, which lends support 
9  to the good faith of Defendant’s effort to add these counterclaims in this matter. The 
10  Court’s failure to find bad faith weighs toward granting the Motion.      
11       D.   Futility                                                        
12       Defendant contends that its proposed counterclaims are not futile because they plead 
13  recognized causes of action that it supports with substantial allegations of fact. Mot. at 15. 
14  Plaintiff argues that (1) Defendant’s proposed breach of contract counterclaim is futile 
15  because it failed to sufficiently plead necessary elements, and (2) Defendant’s proposed 
16  declaratory judgment counterclaim is futile because it is duplicative to Plaintiff’s claim and 
17  serves no useful purpose. Oppo. at 14–17.                                 
18       A motion to amend may be denied if the amendment would be futile or subject to 
19  dismissal. Saul v. United States, 928 F.2d 829, 843 (9th Cir. 1991) (citations omitted).  
20  “[A]  proposed  amendment  is  futile  only  if  no  set  of  facts  can  be  proved  under  the 
21  amendment to the pleadings that would constitute a valid and sufficient claim or defense.” 
22  Miller v. Rykoff-Sexton, Inc., 845 F.2d 209, 214 (9th Cir. 1988), implied overruling on 
23  other grounds by Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009). However, denying leave to amend 
24  for futility is “rare and courts generally defer consideration of challenges to the merits of a 
25                                                                            

26                                                                            
27  2 A compulsory counterclaim is one that “arises out of the transaction or occurrence that is 
   the subject matter of the opposing party’s claim” and “does not require adding another 
28                                                                            
1  proposed amended pleading until after leave to amend is granted and the amended pleading 
2  is filed.” Duhn Oil Tool, Inc. v. Cooper Cameron Corp., No. CV-F-05-1411 OWW/GSA, 
3  2010 WL 596312, at *14 (E.D. Cal. Feb. 16, 2010) (citing Netbula, LLC v. Distinct Corp., 
4  212 F.R.D. 534, 539 (N.D. Cal. 2003)).                                    
5            1.   Proposed Breach of Contract Counterclaim                   
6       Defendant’s  proposed  breach  of  contract  counterclaim  alleges  that  Plaintiff 
7  “breached the terms and conditions of the Agreement by failing to deliver marketable 
8  goods  and  maintain  the  required  trademarks  in  accordance  to  the  Agreement.”  ECF  
9  No. 14-2 at 10. The term it cites as the relevant term for the breach involving marketable 
10  goods is titled “Defective Product Returns” and states that the Distributor (Defendant) may 
11  return to Plaintiff for credit any defective products timely returned to the Distributor by its 
12  customers. Id. at 6. Plaintiff argues Defendant fails to sufficiently plead whether either 
13  party performed its contractual obligations as to that term. Oppo. at 15–16. Plaintiff also 
14  attests that it has located “dozens of documents confirming that it accepted returns for the 
15  wristbands and issued credits to Slow Gold for each and every one of those returns.” 
16  Altomare Decl. ¶ 11.                                                      
17       The Court finds that Defendant’s proposed counterclaim is not entirely clear as to 
18  how Plaintiff breached the contract by failing to deliver marketable goods. The proposed 
19  counterclaim contains allegations that Plaintiff did not “cure its defects,” “continuously 
20  failed to produce quality goods,” and “failed to reimburse [Defendant] for expenses and 
21  damages incurred as a result of [Plaintiff’s] breaches of the Agreement.” ECF No. 14-2  
22  at 7. These allegations fail to specify the actions that breached the “Defective Product 
23  Returns” term in the agreement but could possibly relate to actions relevant to the term. 
24  Therefore, the Court cannot find that no set of facts can be proved that would constitute a 
25  sufficient claim, and so finds it would be more appropriately suited to a motion made after 
26  leave to amend is granted and the amended answer is filed. See Duhn Oil Tool, Inc.,  
27  2010 WL 596312, at *14. This lack of futility weighs toward granting the Motion as to this 
28  breach of contract counterclaim based on a failure by Plaintiff to deliver marketable goods. 
1       Defendant’s proposed counterclaim also alleges Plaintiff breached the contract by 
2  failing to “maintain the required trademarks in accordance to the Agreement” when it failed 
3  to “secure any trademark rights for the marks in the Territory, either through the European 
4  Union Intellectual Property Office, or in any countries or territories specifically mentioned 
5  with the Agreement.” ECF No. 14-2 at 8, 10. It cites two terms in the agreement as relevant 
6  to  this  allegation  titled  “Pacific’s  Marks”  and  “Intellectual  Property  Ownership.”  
7  Id. at 7–8. These terms govern the ownership and use of Plaintiff’s intellectual property as 
8  to the goods, such as trademarks, service marks, trade names, etc. Id. Plaintiff argues that 
9  this allegation is futile because Defendant fails to plead that securing trademark rights was 
10  a requirement of the agreement, nor how it suffered any damages as a result of this alleged 
11  failure. Oppo. at 16–17. Defendant does not address these arguments in its Reply.  
12       The Court agrees with Plaintiff that Defendant has failed to state that there was a 
13  requirement for Plaintiff to secure trademark rights or that it suffered damages as a result. 
14  Without this requirement, no set of facts can be shown to prove that there was a breach, 
15  and this counterclaim would therefore be futile. See Miller, 845 F.2d at 214. The Court’s 
16  finding  of  futility  weighs  toward  denying  the  Motion  as  to  this  breach  of  contract 
17  counterclaim based on a failure by Plaintiff to maintain required trademarks. 
18            2.   Proposed Declaratory Judgment Counterclaim                 
19       Defendant’s  proposed  declaratory  judgment  counterclaim  alleges  that  it  is  not 
20  infringing on Plaintiff’s rights in any trademark because Plaintiff lacks a valid, registered 
21  trademark and because Defendant’s sales predominantly take place in Europe, with little 
22  or no impact on U.S. commerce. ECF No. 14-2 at 11–12. Plaintiff argues that its complaint 
23  includes claims of federal trademark infringement and California common law trademark 
24  infringement, which will result in the same declaration that Defendant seeks, “specifically 
25  whether infringement is occurring.” Oppo. at 15. Plaintiff contends that declaratory relief 
26  is futile, duplicative, and serves no useful purpose. Id. Defendant does not address this 
27  argument in its Reply.                                                    
28                                                                            
1       “[D]eclaratory  relief  is  appropriate  (1)  when  the  judgment  will  serve  a  useful 
2  purpose in clarifying and settling the legal relations in issue, and (2) when it will terminate 
3  and  afford  relief  from  the  uncertainty,  insecurity,  and  controversy  giving  rise  to  the 
4  proceeding.”  Eureka  Fed.  Sav.  &  Loan  Ass'n  v.  Am.  Cas.  Co.  of  Reading,  Pa.,  
5  873 F.2d 229, 231 (9th Cir. 1989) (internal quotation marks and citation omitted). 
6       The Court finds that the proposed declaratory judgment counterclaim would clearly 
7  be subject to dismissal. Defendant’s proposed counterclaim is duplicative to Plaintiff’s 
8  third  and  fourth  causes  of  action  for  federal  trademark  infringement  and  California 
9  common law trademark infringement. See ECF No. 1-2 at 13–15. Thus, the proposed 
10  counterclaim will serve no useful purpose “in clarifying and settling the legal relations in 
11  issue” because the issue of trademark infringement is already before the Court in Plaintiff’s 
12  complaint. See Sliding Door Co. v. KLS Doors, LLC, No. EDCV 13-00196 JGB, 2013 WL 
13  2090298, at *4 (C.D. Cal. May 1, 2013) (dismissing declaratory judgment counterclaim 
14  for non-infringement of patent because it was duplicative to Plaintiff’s cause of action for 
15  patent infringement and thus failed to serve any useful purpose); Capitol Recs., Inc. v. 
16  Weed, No. 206-CV-01124-PHX-JAT, 2008 WL 1820667, at *3 (D. Ariz. Apr. 22, 2008) 
17  (denying motion for leave to amend answer to add counterclaim for declaratory judgment 
18  of non-infringement because it did not allege any issues that would not already be litigated 
19  in the plaintiff’s case in chief and in the defendant’s own affirmative defenses). The Court’s 
20  finding that it would clearly be subject to dismissal weighs toward denying the Motion as 
21  to this declaratory judgment counterclaim. See Saul, 928 F.2d at 843.     
22       Considering all the Foman factors, the Court finds they weigh toward granting in 
23  part and denying in part Defendant’s Motion. The Court finds no prejudice to Plaintiff in 
24  allowing Defendant to add its proposed counterclaims, but it also finds some of the 
25  counterclaims would be futile or subject to dismissal. Accordingly, the Court finds it 
26  appropriate to grant leave to amend the answer to add only the proposed counterclaims that 
27  are  not  futile  or  subject  to  dismissal.  See  Bonin  v.  Calderon,  59  F.3d  815,  845  
28                                                                            
1          Cir.  1995) (“Futility of amendment can, by itself, justify the denial of a motion for 
2 || leave to amend.”); Saul, 928 F.2d at 843. 
3           CONCLUSION 
4         Based  on the  above,  the  Court  GRANTS  IN  PART  AND  DENIES  IN  PART 
5 || Defendant Slow Gold Limited’s Motion for Leave to File Counterclaims as follows: 
6         1.     The Court GRANTS the Motion for leave to amend the answer to include a 
7    counterclaim for breach of contract based on a  failure by Plaintiff to deliver marketable 
8 || goods. 
9         2.     The Court DENIES the Motion for leave to amend the answer to include a 
10   |}counterclaim for breach of contract based on a failure by Plaintiff to maintain trademarks. 
11         3.     The Court DENIES the Motion for leave to amend the answer to include a 
12 || counterclaim for declaratory judgment of non-infringement of trademark. 
13         4.     Defendant shall file its amended answer in conformance with this Order on or 
14 || before February 17, 2023. 
15         IT IS SO ORDERED. 
16 || Dated:  February 10, 2023                     NO 
17                                             DE 
18                                           Honorable Linda Lopez 
19                                           United States District Judge

12       The Court will next consider the Foman factors of undue delay, bad faith or dilatory 
13  motive, futility of amendment, and prejudice to the opposing party.

18  that Defendant has failed to provide a reasonable explanation for filing this Motion four 
19  months after it filed its answer when the counterclaims are based on facts and theories 
20  Defendant knew or should have known at the time it filed its answer. Oppo. at 11. Plaintiff

21       C.   Bad Faith                                                       
22       Defendant contends that it brings this Motion in good faith because its counterclaims 
23  have merit and directly relate to the contract at issue in Plaintiff’s complaint. Mot. at 9. 
24  Plaintiff argues that Defendant has shown bad faith by misstating Plaintiff’s purported 
25  “consent” to add counterclaims and for delaying its filing of this Motion in an effort to 
26  harass Plaintiff and/or increase the costs of litigation. Oppo. at 13.    
27       The Court does not find that Plaintiff has established that Defendant has acted in bad 
28  faith.  Although  Defendant  may  have  misstated  Plaintiff’s  purported  consent  to  the 
1  counterclaims, the Court has not considered or relied on the purported consent in its 
2  analysis. The Court has already found that although Defendant could have filed this Motion 
3  earlier, the delay was not unreasonable, and it was timely according to the parties’ case 
4  scheduling order. Furthermore, the parties appear to agree that Defendant’s proposed 
5  counterclaims are compulsory.2 Mot. at 12; Oppo. at 5. The Court agrees that Defendant’s 
6  proposed counterclaims are compulsory because they arise out of the agreement that is the 
7  subject  matter  of  Plaintiff’s  complaint.  If  Defendant  fails  to  plead  a  compulsory 
8  counterclaim, it will be precluded from asserting it in a separate action, which lends support 
9  to the good faith of Defendant’s effort to add these counterclaims in this matter. The 
10  Court’s failure to find bad faith weighs toward granting the Motion.      
11       D.   Futility                                                        
12       Defendant contends that its proposed counterclaims are not futile because they plead 
13  recognized causes of action that it supports with substantial allegations of fact. Mot. at 15. 
14  Plaintiff argues that (1) Defendant’s proposed breach of contract counterclaim is futile 
15  because it failed to sufficiently plead necessary elements, and (2) Defendant’s proposed 
16  declaratory judgment counterclaim is futile because it is duplicative to Plaintiff’s claim and 
17  serves no useful purpose. Oppo. at 14–17.                                 
18       A motion to amend may be denied if the amendment would be futile or subject to 
19  dismissal. Saul v. United States,

21  amendment to the pleadings that would constitute a valid and sufficient claim or defense.”

 (9th Cir. 1988), implied overruling on 
23  other grounds by Ashcroft v. Iqbal,
556 U.S. 662
